tasks.short: Check deliveries, label parts, put them away, locate parts for customers, count stock, decide reorders and send orders.

steps.what: Parts salesperson checks delivered parts against the packing slip
Parts salesperson labels parts with stock number and bin location
Parts salesperson puts parts away in their bins
Parts salesperson locates parts on the shelves for customers
Parts salesperson counts stock and corrects the inventory records
Parts salesperson checks stock levels and decides what to reorder
Parts salesperson phones or e-mails orders to the wholesaler

tasks.design: Deliveries are scanned against the wholesaler's electronic delivery note in the store system ({OPS_SYSTEM}), and a label printer prints stock number and bin location from each scan. Counts are done with a handheld scanner. The system proposes reorders for parts below their minimum; after the salesperson checks the list, it sends the order to the wholesaler's portal ({PARTNER_PORTAL}). Putting away and picking parts stay manual.
tasks.previous_blocker: Deliveries were ticked off on paper, labels written and orders phoned.
tasks.enabler_now: Wholesalers send electronic delivery notes and take orders through portals.
tasks.still_hard: Mislabelled bins and wrong counts still need someone to look.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which slow part to keep anyway because a regular customer needs it.

reach.learn: Whether reorder proposals cut emergency orders.

evidence.claim: Electronic delivery notes, label printers and handheld scanners for counts are standard in parts stores.
Per-person scan logs can monitor staff, so the works council must consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from delivery to the wholesaler order; payment of invoices is outside.
Input contract: delivery notes sent by the wholesaler; minimum stock levels set by the store manager; fallback is paper and phone.
Putting away and picking do not change.
Scan logs are about stock, not used to rate staff.
research_questions: Do stock differences at year-end fall?

already_counted.description: Parts salesperson checks the reorder proposal.

incremental.description: Store manager keeps minimum stock levels current.

approvals.approved_version: The reorder list as checked by the salesperson in s6; changes need a new check before sending.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Small stores with few deliveries save less.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Enter parts in the till, add warranty and return terms, confirm with the customer, issue the slip and file copies for the books.

steps.what: Parts salesperson enters parts and quantities in the till
Parts salesperson writes warranty and return terms on larger sales contracts
Parts salesperson goes through the sale with the customer and confirms it
Parts salesperson writes out the sales slip by hand for account customers
Parts salesperson files copies of slips for the bookkeeping

tasks.design: Parts found in the catalogue lookup go into the sale in the store system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) with one scan or click, and larger sales get a contract from a template with the standard warranty and return terms, which the salesperson checks. After the salesperson confirms the sale with the customer, the system prints or e-mails the slip or contract and posts the sale to the ledger in the {ERP}.
tasks.previous_blocker: Account sales were written on paper slips and copies filed for the bookkeeper.
tasks.enabler_now: Store systems print or e-mail slips from the sale and post sales to the ledger.
tasks.still_hard: Special terms for trade customers need a person to check.
tasks.human_edge: Explaining warranty terms so a customer trusts the shop.

reach.learn: Whether posted sales cut month-end work.

evidence.claim: Store systems print or e-mail sales slips and post sales to the ledger.
Businesses must keep sales records for seven years for tax purposes.

assumptions: Boundary: from parts picked to sales posted; payment collection is outside.
Input contract: warranty and return terms set by the store manager; account customers kept in the store system; fallback is paper slips.
Confirming with the customer does not change.
Bookkeeper time is outside the salesperson's savings.

incremental.description: Parts salesperson fixes failed e-mails of slips.

approvals.approved_version: The sales slip lines, prices and account as confirmed with the customer in s3; any change needs a new confirmation before the slip is issued.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Stores that already print slips from the till save less.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Get the vehicle details, search the catalogue, cross-reference numbers, look up price and stock and confirm the part with the customer.

steps.what: Parts salesperson asks the customer for make, model, year and engine
Parts salesperson reads catalogs and computer displays to find the replacement part
Parts salesperson cross-references maker numbers to the shop's stock numbers
Parts salesperson looks up prices and stock for the part
Parts salesperson confirms the part with the customer

tasks.design: The salesperson enters the number plate, and the parts catalogue ({OTHER}) decodes the vehicle and filters parts by fitment, so fewer questions about make and engine are needed. The store system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) maps maker numbers to the shop's stock numbers and shows price and stock with each match. Confirming the part with the customer stays in person.
tasks.previous_blocker: Vehicle details were asked one by one and numbers cross-referenced in printed lists.
tasks.enabler_now: Parts catalogues find parts by plate, VIN or maker number.
tasks.still_hard: Plate lookups miss modified or imported vehicles; the salesperson still checks.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing that this model year changed the brake supplier halfway.
tasks.altitude: The salesperson checks fitment matches instead of searching.

reach.learn: Whether plate lookups cut wrong parts.

evidence.claim: TecDoc Catalogue finds parts by VIN, plate or OE number.
Algolia auto parts search filters by vehicle fitment and suggests alternatives.
A number plate is personal data once linked to an owner; lookups should use vehicle data only.

assumptions: Boundary: from the customer's request to the confirmed part; ordering is outside.
Input contract: catalogue data from the catalogue supplier; cross-reference table kept by the store system supplier; fallback is printed catalogues.
Confirming with the customer does not change.
Customers' time is outside the salesperson's savings.
research_questions: Do returns for wrong parts fall?

incremental.description: Parts salesperson reports wrong catalogue matches.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Stores with older or unusual vehicles save less.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Hear the malfunction, inspect and photograph the old part, find candidate parts for the fault and decide the replacement with the customer.

steps.what: Parts salesperson listens to the customer's description of the malfunction
Parts salesperson inspects old parts brought in by the customer
Parts salesperson searches for parts that match the described fault

loop.input: The salesperson's note of the customer's fault description and the identified vehicle.
loop.output: Two or three likely part groups, each with the phrase in the description that points to it.
loop.check: Code keeps only parts in those groups that fit the vehicle per the catalogue's fitment data and are in stock or orderable; the salesperson decides which part is needed.
loop.stop: One suggestion per request; no fitting part means the salesperson searches by hand.
loop.why_not_simpler: Customers describe noises and symptoms in their own words; part-group menus do not map them.

steps.what: Parts salesperson determines the replacement parts required with the customer

tasks.design: The salesperson photographs the old part and a photo match in the parts catalogue app ({OTHER}) proposes the item, which the salesperson confirms by looking. For described faults, a bounded step maps the description to likely part groups and code keeps only parts that fit the vehicle and can be supplied. Listening to the customer and deciding the replacement stay with the salesperson; no chatbot talks to customers.
tasks.previous_blocker: Old parts were matched by eye against catalogues and faults by memory.
tasks.enabler_now: Photo recognition of parts exists in beta, and fitment data check suggestions.
tasks.still_hard: Worn or dirty parts defeat photo matching; a wrong fault guess wastes a customer's money.
tasks.human_edge: Asking the one question that tells a worn bearing from a loose shield.
tasks.altitude: The salesperson checks suggested parts instead of searching from memory.

reach.learn: Whether photo matching works on dirty parts.

evidence.claim: The Kramp app recognises products from a photo, in beta.
TecDoc Catalogue finds parts by VIN, plate or OE number.

assumptions: Boundary: from the customer's request to the decided replacement; fitting the part is outside.
Input contract: fitment and stock data from the parts catalogue and store system; fallback is searching by hand.
Listening and deciding do not change.
Photo matching is used only where the catalogue supports it.
unknowns: Share of requests with an old part or a fault description.
research_questions: How often is the first suggested part group right?

already_counted.description: Parts salesperson checks photo matches and suggested parts.

incremental.description: Parts salesperson takes a photo of each old part.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Most of this task is listening and judging.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The parts salesperson keeps the conversation and every choice of part; lookups, slips and paper stock records shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A salesperson who finds the right part on the first try for nearly every customer.
